title: Multilingual Embedding Corpus Sampling and Regression Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures our recommended corpus design, sampling heuristics, and regression test harness for multilingual embedding onboarding. It is intended as a working playbook used by Applied ML engineers when creating new evaluation sets for semantic search, clustering sanity checks, and cross-lingual retrieval probes.

Scope and goals:
- Provide repeatable dataset construction recipes that balance coverage (domains, languages, genres) with annotation cost.
- Define probe types and metric thresholds that catch regressions likely to affect product SLAs (top-k retrieval, clustering quality, cross-lingual parity).
- Describe CI integration for embedding regressions, including failure modes and triage guidance.

High-level principles:
1) Keep evaluation slices small and focused: each probe should test a single property (e.g., paraphrase robustness, length-invariance, domain drift).
2) Mix real-world and synthetic examples: real samples find realistic distributional failures; controlled synthetic perturbations isolate brittleness.
3) Language balance by risk tier: prioritize high-traffic languages (en, fr, de, es, pt, ja, ko, zh) for richer sampling and lower-traffic languages for spot checks.
4) Reproducible sampling: store deterministic seeds and sampling queries so sets can be rebuilt.

Dataset composition recommendations:
- Total corpus per onboarding: target 3k-10k annotated pairs depending on scope.
  - Semantic search relevance (pairwise relevance judgments): 1.5k–5k pairs across domains.
  - Clustering sanity (labelled clusters): 500–2k documents covering 8–20 clusters per language.
  - Cross-lingual retrieval probes: ~500 parallel or comparable-document pairs per language pair.
  - Robustness probes (noise, truncation, paraphrase): 1k synthetic variants.
- Domain stratification: ensure minimum representation from product, documentation, marketing, support, and user-generated content where applicable.
- Document length buckets: short (<64 tokens), medium (64–256), long (>256) with at least 20% in long bucket for long-context workloads.
- Metadata capture: language, source domain, length_bucket, original_uri, sampling_seed, annotator_id (if human-reviewed). Always store as flat CSV/TSV metadata for easy filtering.

Language and cross-lingual sampling heuristics:
- For high-priority languages, sample from in-house traffic logs + open datasets (CC100/MUSE-derived) while respecting privacy.
- Use machine translation as a controlled augmentation: translate 200–500 English queries to target languages, then back-translate for paraphrase pairs. Mark synthetic vs. natural in metadata.
- For low-resource languages, prioritize cluster-based sampling: cluster multilingual crawl and sample cluster centroids to maximize lexical variety.

Probe types and concrete templates:
1) Semantic relevance probes
   - Query-oriented pairs (query, doc): label as relevant / partially / irrelevant.
   - Metrics: P@1, P@5, MRR, Recall@100 where applicable.
   - Failure modes to catch: ranking inversions, topical drift, language mismatch.

2) Paraphrase & paraphrase-robustness probes
   - Generate paraphrase variants using N-shot prompts + model-based paraphrasers; include human-verified subset.
   - Metrics: cosine gap between paraphrase pairs (expect high similarity), retrieval recall when using paraphrase as query.

3) Clustering sanity checks
   - Labelled clusters with human-provided cluster ids; evaluate NMI, ARI, average intra-cluster cosine, and cluster purity at k.
   - Use notion of "sanity failure" when NMI drops by >0.08 vs baseline or when average intra-cluster cosine decreases by >0.07.

4) Cross-lingual retrieval probes
   - Source query in language A, gold doc in language B; measure cross-lingual retrieval recall and mean rank.
   - Target metric: delta vs monolingual baseline should be within tolerance (e.g., <10% relative drop for high-priority languages).

5) Robustness/noise perturbations
   - Token-level noise (random deletion, swap), punctuation stripping, casing changes, unicode variants.
   - Metrics: similarity delta distribution; flag examples where similarity drops below acceptable per-language thresholds.

Annotation and quality control:
- Use a small pool of trusted annotators (5–8) for final judgements. Capture inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff alpha) per slice; if alpha < 0.6, rework instructions.
- Annotation UI: present pairs in isolation, randomize order, allow partial relevance. Include examples and edge-case guidance in the UI.

Regression harness and CI integration:
- Baseline generation: for each onboarding set, store a baseline embedding dump (vector files + metadata) from the model version used in production when the dataset was created.
- CI job structure:
  - nightly/regression job computes metrics on the evaluation corpus and compares to baseline.
  - Thresholds configured per-metric and per-slice in YAML (example config path: /infra/emb-regression/configs/<dataset>.yml).
  - On threshold breach: create Jira ticket with diff summary, top failing examples, and links to artifact dumps.
- Lightweight regression mode: sampled checks that run on PRs (subset of 200 pairs across slices) to give early feedback.
- Heavy regression mode: full run triggered on major model/quantization changes.

Failure triage playbook:
1) Check whether regression is uniform across languages or concentrated. If concentrated, suspect tokenization or language-modeling mismatch.
2) Inspect clustering metrics: if clustering collapses, evaluate embedding norm distributions and debug quantization ramps.
3) Verify that baseline and new vectors used identical pre/post-processing (tokenization, pooling).
4) Re-run on raw text with an isolated inference runtime to rule out runtime-level batching/caching bugs.

Acceptance criteria for onboarding (example):
- Semantic retrieval: P@5 within 3% absolute of baseline or better for each high-priority language.
- Clustering: NMI drop <= 0.05 vs baseline for majority of languages; no language with drop >0.08 without mitigation.
- Cross-lingual recall: relative drop <12% for top-tier languages.
- Paraphrase robustness: 90th percentile cosine similarity above model-specific threshold (store per-model table).

Quick checklist (when creating a new embedding corpus):
- [ ] Define business use-cases and list target languages and domains.
- [ ] Create deterministic sampling queries and save seeds.
- [ ] Partition by length and domain buckets; export metadata TSV.
- [ ] Generate synthetic perturbations and mark them.
- [ ] Run local clustering sanity check and record metrics.
- [ ] Add dataset config to regression YAML and register baseline vectors.
- [ ] Run PR-level lightweight regression and review top failures.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide acceptable thresholds for low-resource languages (action: discuss on 2026-03 eng-applied-ml sync).
- Explore use of small supervised contrastive finetuning as a pre-regression filter to reduce churn for minor model updates.
- Automate sample selection for lightweight PR checks to maximize failure detection while keeping runtime <10 minutes.

Appendix: example metric thresholds (placeholders)
- P@1 baseline tolerance: 0.02 absolute
- P@5 baseline tolerance: 0.03 absolute
- NMI clustering tolerance: 0.05 absolute
- Cross-lingual recall tolerance: 0.12 relative

Notes to self (working):
- Keep this doc intentionally prescriptive but leave examples minimal; link to actual dataset manifests in linked_artifacts.
- When adding final templates, include a short sample YAML for regression config and a micro-schema for vector storage (tsv + npy pairing).

End of playbook.
